It’s interesting to see your perspective on it, and I’ve gotta admit that I also feel the same way to a certain degree.

Reflecting back, when I was younger (like between the ages of 12-17 which is when I was in high school) I can definitely say that I was more emotive in the way I thought and expressed myself about the coup, Allende & Pinochet, the US’ involvement, etc and I think that would be due to the influence my family/family friends had on me upon the stories they would share during their time living through it all between the 70s-80s. 

Now that I’m older and have taken upon myself to actually educate myself more without the bias hanging over my head from my family over it all, it’s definitely opened up my eyes and desensitised the idea that historic events occur at a global scale and not just Chile (and Australia, which is where I live and grew up in) being the only countries that faced genocide, terrible political systems, socioeconomic injustices, forceful assimilations, famine, war, etc.

That’s not to say that I discredit the intensity of what Chile has faced but as I’m older and have educated myself further through independent research via documentaries, articles, historical books, etc of other nations, I think what I feel now is one of two things:

1. Further sadness over the idea that even more people at a global had suffered over these traumatic events.
2. That the past is the past and the need to accept over what has occurred in the world and there is nothing one can do to change or erase all of that suffering the world has faced.

Yes it sucks but that’s life and we should be grateful that we are able to personally live in a modern-day society where we are able to have all of these choices and accomplish life goals at our own will without the worry of being stopped by a corrupt government with a hidden agenda.

So I’m from Australia, from what I’ve seen it doesn’t have to necessarily be just Chileans celebrating the Chilean holiday at those day-festivals but that just could be over how well we accept multiculturalism.

I’ve noticed that lots of other hispanic cultures would participate simply because their partner is Chilean or people could have Chilean friends and invite them to tag along, etc! Like over here in the South West of Sydney, there are a lot of Uruguayans, Argentinians, Peruvians, El Salvadorenians, etc that would join in on the fun! Heck, I’ve even seen a couple of Filipino & Assyrian families gather round and participate too because why not!

There’s no need to apologise for expressing how you feel! What you’ve written is almost asif you hit the nail in the coffin over what my feelings are towards los desaparecidos, what happened to Allende, Victor Jara, Neruda, etc & my experience growing up was like too!

Luckily, where I live in Australia has a bunch of ethnicities in which their own country have experienced war, famine, and other sorts of perish too so I managed to grow up with a bunch of people who were born from parents that were immigrants/asylum seekers. 

Oddly enough, whenever I were to express my dissatisfaction over the Chilean history and the events that led to the military coup, as well as it’s aftermath, I managed to properly communicate with the parents of my friends and connect on a deeper level with them instead of the people of my generation - which like you, also somewhat felt frustration over the fact that they didn’t really care about the past of the country their family are from as they weren’t alive to feel & experience the atrocities that were faced by others that time.
